Its tone is slightly nasal, with a strong Middle Eastern character. The range sits mainly in the upper middle register, high and ringing and full of expression. Its resonance comes chiefly from the tube itself, and the way the double reed vibrates gives the sound a grainy edge. Compared with the Western oboe, the mizmar is rougher and more forceful; compared with the dizi, its tone is heavier and more husky. This particular sound makes it indispensable to Middle Eastern folk music and traditional celebration, where it is used to build a lively, joyful atmosphere.

The mizmar is an aerophone of the Arab music of the Middle East, North Africa and West Asia, Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.112.2, a general term for single- or double-reed pipe playing; in Egypt and the Levant it usually means the conical shawm, while Turkey and Armenia call the instrument zurna. It is traditionally made from a single piece of apricot or plum wood, and metal versions also exist; the body is about thirty to forty centimetres long, with seven finger holes and one thumb hole, and a double reed joined to the mouthpiece through a small bocal. Musicians in Egypt and the Levant often play in groups of two or three, together with one or two double-headed bass drums, for weddings, belly-dance accompaniment, festivals, traditional wedding celebrations and dances such as the dabke.
米茲瑪爾是起源於中東與北非地區的傳統雙簧管樂器，名稱源自阿拉伯語。該樂器可追溯至: The mizmar is a traditional double-reed instrument that originated in the Middle East and North Africa, and its name comes from Arabic. It can be traced back to the civilisations of ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, where it was first used in religious ritual and royal celebration. In the Islamic Golden Age the making and playing of the mizmar developed to a high level, and it gradually became an important part of Arab, Persian and Turkish musical culture.
